voice.text: Summer is hot. Winter is cold. [pause] Why? Tap your guess: does your half of Earth lean toward the sun in summer — or does the whole Earth move closer to the sun?
Two dances at once! The moon <emphasis>revolves around Earth</emphasis> — one lap takes about a month. [pause] And all the while, Earth carries the moon along on its year-long trip around the sun.
Here is a secret: the moon makes <emphasis>no light of its own</emphasis>. None! [pause] Moonlight is sunlight, bouncing off gray rock. The moon is a giant mirror in the sky.

The sun always lights one half of the moon. As the moon circles Earth, we see that lit half from different angles. [pause] Between the moon and the sun? We see the dark side — new moon. Off to the side? Half lit — first quarter. Opposite the sun? The whole lit face — full moon. Then last quarter, and around again. [pause] It is like walking around a lamp-lit ball.

Now the big one. Why summer? <emphasis>Not</emphasis> because Earth gets closer to the sun! [pause] Earth is tilted, like a leaning top. When your half leans toward the sun, sunlight hits it strong and long — summer. When your half leans away — winter. [pause] In fact, Earth is slightly farther from the sun during our summer. The tilt does it all.
The moon even moves our oceans. Its gravity gently tugs the sea toward it, making the water rise and fall at the shore. [pause] High tide, low tide — about twice every day.

And the moon itself? It is the closest thing to us in space — much closer than the sun. About one quarter Earth's width. [pause] No air, no wind, no rain — just old, cratered rock. An astronaut's footprint up there can last millions of years.
Build the moon's month! Tap the phase that comes next, starting from the new moon: new, first quarter, full, last quarter.
Why is it summer? Tilt, or distance? [pause] Think hard — this one fools a lot of grown-ups.
Now moonlight, phases, and tides. Look at the picture when there is one, and think about where the light comes from.
All done, moon watcher! [pause] Now show what you know.
Not quite. The order is: new, first quarter, full, last quarter — growing, then shrinking.
Not quite. Distance is not the cause — remember, Earth is even a little farther away in our summer. Think about the tilt.
Not quite. The moon is cold gray rock. Its light is bounced sunlight.
Not quite. Earth's shadow only touches the moon at a rare eclipse. Phases come from the angle we see.
Not quite. Look again: how much of the moon's lit half can you see?
Not quite. Wind makes waves on top. The tide is the moon's gravity, tugging the whole sea.
Not quite. Watch the moon for two weeks — its shape changes a little every single night.
Why is it summer where you live?
Why does the moon shine at night?
What makes the moon's phases?
The new moon starts to grow. Which phase comes next?
What makes the sea rise and fall twice a day?
<soft>You know our closest neighbor!</soft> [pause] Well done, moon watcher.
Good try! Let's watch the tilt, and the phases, once more.
Lesson done! Tonight, look up, and draw the moon's shape in your log.
